en:
...So, it's finally my turn to speak.
My name is Shoji Arai.
I'm a second-year.
Tell me, do you all like movies?
I love them.
French films in particular.
European cinema is wonderful, isn't it?
The images are beautiful and poetic; they cleanse the soul.
What about you, {a}?{p}Do you like French films?
I like them
I don't like them
Neither, really
I've never seen one

...What a pitiful person you are.
To think you've never yet encountered such splendor.
You really must see one.
I'm sure you'll come to love them.
...Could it be, {a}, that you dislike movies in general?
I like movies
I don't like movies
Neither, really

Oh, is that so?
You like movies, and yet you don't watch French films.
What an odd person you are.
But then, everyone is different.{p}
So, what genre of movies do you like?
Action
Sci-fi/Horror
Suspense
Love/Romance
Drama
Comedy

Hm hm... So you like sci-fi and horror?
You have rather bad taste, don't you?{p}

I don't much care for that type of film myself.
Above all, they have no class.
The story is just tacked on as an afterthought, and far too many of them rely on nothing but visual shocks and special effects.
...But movies are frightening, aren't they?
No, I don't mean horror movies.
I mean film itself.
Don't you think so?
People have long said that photographs steal a person's soul, haven't they?
Nowadays we laugh that off as superstition, but back then people seriously believed it.
That every photo taken of you shortened your life, or that when three people are photographed together, the one in the middle dies young.
Back then, I suppose photography must have seemed utterly uncanny.
Your own image, sealed inside a single sheet of paper.
It truly was magic.
And so everyone feared it.
It's the same with movies.
When movies were first born, they caused quite a stir.
For example, a character in a film fires a gun right at the screen, you see?
They say the audience watching it fainted, thinking they'd been shot dead.
People even believed that other people lived beyond that silver screen, and that they were watching the world those people lived in.
Nowadays no one believes that, of course.
...But is it really a lie?
Was what people believed back then truly just their imagination?
I can't quite bring myself to think so.
Sometimes film captures things that should never be filmed, or strange things that don't exist in reality...
I can't shake the feeling that film has that kind of uncanny power.
What I'm about to tell you is the story of one such movie.{p}

There was a boy in my class named Yasuo Tokita.
He loved movies like no one else, and he often talked to me about them.
And my, did he know a lot.
A real film fanatic, I suppose you'd call him.
I thought I knew quite a lot myself, but there's always someone better.
He had me beat.
There was hardly a movie he hadn't seen.
Even when I did desperate research, trying to show him up, it was no use.
There's the expression "walking encyclopedia," and when it came to movies, that's exactly what he was.
Being such a movie lover, Tokita deeply regretted that our school had no film club of any kind.
After all, his dream, of course, was to become a film director.
So he went and started one himself.
Back then, we were first-years.{p}

Even so, Tokita actively reached out to upperclassmen and teachers, and in no time at all he'd founded a film society.
Naturally, it couldn't become an official club right away.
It turns out there are quite a lot of movie lovers, if you look for them.
All told, about twenty people joined, I heard.
He was overjoyed.{p}

He brought most of the filming equipment himself.
Though by equipment, I just mean an 8mm camera and some simple lighting gear.
And by 8mm, I don't mean the kind of video camera everyone uses now.
I mean an old-fashioned handheld 8mm film camera.
You don't see many of those these days.
Even so, the members were thrilled, I hear.
After all, they got to play at making a real movie.
They felt a bit like professionals.{p}

Hm?
Me?
Did I join that Film Research Society, you ask?
No, I didn't.
I was in the soccer club, you see.
Is it funny, me being in the soccer club?
Well, that's a story for another time.
By the way, what about you?{p}Would you be interested in a film research society?
I'm interested
I'm not interested

I see.
So you're interested.
Then if it were you, what job would you want to take on?
There are so many jobs in filmmaking, after all.{p}
Actor
Director
Cameraman
Producer
Screenwriter
Behind-the-scenes crew

Oh, you're quite the connoisseur.
Well, whether a movie turns out good or bad is decided almost entirely by the director.{p}

But it seems most people say actor.
Actors stand out, after all; it's flashy and glamorous.
And the actors are the ones who become popular.
If you screened your own movie at the school festival, whoever played the lead would become a star.
Provided the movie was any good, of course.
Starstruck types watch movies for the actors.
But connoisseurs watch them for the director.
Naturally, Tokita wanted to direct.
Well, I suppose most of the people who joined were the starstruck type.{p}

And so filming began on the society's memorable first production.
I think it was right around this time last year.
...You said you like horror and sci-fi movies, didn't you?
As it happens, so did he.
The movie he set out to make was a horror film titled 'The Mummy Man and the Beauty.'
Now, don't laugh at the title.
What he wanted to make wasn't one of today's SFX films loaded with special effects; if anything, he wanted to make an old-fashioned monster movie from the golden age.
Not that he could have pulled off flashy special effects even if he'd tried.
So instead of fussing over that sort of thing, he poured himself into dark direction and atmosphere, so that even a cheap monster in a simple costume and makeup would look real.{p}

He worked truly hard at it.
People who are eager at first gradually lose interest; that's how it goes.
In the end, they only do what they want to, and won't touch anything that bores them or takes real work.
Most of them had joined half for fun, after all.
Even so, Tokita kept at it, helped by the very few who shared his ambition, handling everything from odd jobs to acting.
In my heart, I was cheering him on.
What was the movie about?
Tokita wrote the script too.
The basic plot goes like this.{p}

A mummy brought over from Egypt comes back to life and searches for the reincarnation of the princess it once served.
In the end, it turns her into a mummy too, places her in its own coffin with it, and the two of them return to Egypt together.
Simple, isn't it?
Well, the actors were all hams.
And they were students, too.
Most of it is set in the school.
So the heroine is a student at this school, too, wearing a sailor uniform.
And she's supposed to be the reincarnation of an Egyptian princess.
Rather a dubious premise, isn't it?
Even so, somehow or other, they finished filming.{p}

But that's when the hard part begins.
You probably think that once you've shot it, the movie is done, but you'd be dead wrong.
Whether it turns out interesting or not depends entirely on the editing that comes next.
You take all the scattered scenes captured on the film you've shot and splice them together, one by one.
And then a single movie is complete.
Apparently, it's work that takes a great deal of patience.
Though for someone who loves it, I suppose it's irresistibly fun.
And Tokita was one of those people.
He threw himself into the editing, losing all track of time.{p}

"...Huh?
That's weird.
Did I shoot a scene like this?"
Looking at one of the reels, he tilted his head, puzzled.
It was a scene with the Mummy Man.
The scene where the Mummy Man lumbers around in the dark, searching for the reincarnated princess.
He had indeed shot a similar scene, but this one matched neither his memory nor his storyboards.
When you make a movie, you first draw up what's called a storyboard.
Then you shoot each scene to match it.
Otherwise, by the time you finish shooting, you can't make heads or tails of anything, and you can't shoot efficiently in the limited time you have.{p}

The film clearly showed the mummy's face.
And it was far more grotesque and realistic than the makeup he had applied.
Even Tokita, who must have seen countless horror movies, felt a chill run down his spine when he saw that film.
That's how well it was shot.
He had no memory of shooting a cut like that.
But maybe he was misremembering.
There was no way Tokita wouldn't use a scene that good.
He edited it in.{p}

But the next day, while looking at some other film, he found yet another scene he didn't remember shooting.
When you shoot a movie, you run many times more film than the actual running time.
So you end up with a huge number of reels.
This was the scene where a detective investigating a mysterious string of murders is killed by the Mummy Man.{p}

Of course, the detective was played by one of the film society members.
The death scene they had actually shot was a simple one.
The detective, attacked by the mummy, runs away.
The mummy's hands reach for the detective's neck, and the screen goes black.
Then comes the detective's scream.{p}
After that, a close-up of the mummy's bloodied hands.{p}

Yet that film clearly showed the detective dying.
And how realistic it was!
The detective barely had any screen time.
You see, the boy who played him was such a terrible actor that they couldn't give him much screen time.
And yet here was an utterly convincing performance.
The detective being strangled by the mummy, his face twisted in agony.
Then a single thread of bright red blood spilling from the corner of his mouth.
The detective collapsing to the ground and going still.
One cut after another like that appeared on the screen.{p}
It was the very next day.
The student who played the detective was killed.
Strangled, you see.

When Tokita heard how it happened, he couldn't believe his ears.
It was exactly like that scene, wasn't it?
Apparently, no one knows who strangled him.
After all, he had been asleep alone in his own room in the middle of the night.
There was no sign that anyone had snuck in, and the room hadn't been disturbed.
So naturally, suspicion falls on the family.
Tokita grew terrified.
What if he had died because Tokita had watched that film...
What if this was the mummy's curse...
What would you think, in his place?
Would you want to keep editing that movie?{p}If you did, something even stranger might show up on the film.
Keep editing
Stop editing now

Hm hm... How cruel you are.
With a personality like that, I won't be responsible for what becomes of you.
But Tokita was the same.
He loved movies to death, after all.
This movie might become a masterpiece for the ages.
When he thought that, he wanted to keep editing more than anything.{p}
And sure enough, the film he watched that day had something even stranger on it.

This time, it was the scene where the heroine, the reincarnated princess, is shut inside the coffin.
In the script, she sees the mummy, faints from sheer terror, and is then shut inside the mummy's coffin.{p}

But what do you know?
What that film showed was a scene of cruelty so savage you'd want to look away.{p}

The mummy squeezed her in its arms so hard that it crushed her insides.
And then, of all things, it began tearing off her arms and legs.
One by one, carefully.
She wasn't dead yet.
She twisted her bloodied body, thrashing desperately to get away from the mummy.
But it was no use.
Once the mummy had torn off every last one of her limbs, it tossed them into the coffin.
Then, at last, it twisted off her head and carelessly threw the rest of her body into the coffin.
And then it rubbed its cheek against her head and hugged it close.{p}

And with that, the film ended.
Tokita stared at the scene, stunned.
There are all sorts of horror movies, and the ones with one bloody scene after another are called splatter films, or gore flicks.
But the images now burned into Tokita's mind were beyond anything such feeble terms could describe.
"...I've never seen a movie like this."
It's strange, considering he was supposedly the one filming it.
The movie had taken on a life of its own.
That's what Tokita thought, and he watched the scene over and over again.
No matter how many times he watched it, it never lost its freshness.{p}

Naturally, he used that scene for the movie's climax.
Of course, there was no way a movie with such extreme gore spliced into it could be screened at school.
Even so, he was satisfied.
He was convinced that, as an independent film, it would succeed wherever he pitched it.{p}
It was the very next day.{p}

...I'm sure you've guessed by now.
The girl who played the heroine was found brutally murdered.
They say her body was in pieces.
Of course, I never heard the details, but Tokita knew.
What state the body was in, and how she was killed.
And that the proof was all recorded on that reel.
It was after school that very day, as I recall.
Tokita came up to me and told me how realistic and amazing this movie was.{p}

"I'm making an amazing movie right now.
It's a masterpiece, no doubt about it.
It's going to go down in history.
...You like movies, don't you?
If you want, I could show you a little of what I'm editing."
That's how I came to hear about this movie.
I gladly tagged along after him.
I was so excited.
...Well?
If you got an invitation like that, would you have high hopes for the movie?{p}Or would you sneer at it, figuring it's just some amateur production anyway?
I'd have high hopes
I'd sneer at it
I can't tell until I see it

The Film Research Society was allowed to use the audiovisual room after school.
It couldn't become an official club yet, you see, so it had no club room of its own.
He began editing with practiced hands.
"Today, as a special treat, I'll show you a new scene before it's been edited.
The climax is ferocious, but you'll have to wait for the finished film to enjoy that."
Then he pulled one reel out of the mountain of film piled up there.{p}

"...I haven't edited this one yet.
Let's watch this one today."{p}

The clapperboard filled the screen, and the acting began.
One blown take followed another, the same scene repeating again and again.
It's fascinating, you know.
"...Ah!"{p}
"...That's me on there.
I have to stop it!

I have to stop it, now!"
I had no idea at all what he was panicking about.{p}
Tokita was frantically trying to stop the editing equipment.
He should have been used to handling machines like that, yet maybe his fingers were shaking, because he didn't seem able to work it properly.{p}
"It won't stop... The machine won't stop!"

His face had gone deathly pale.
Startled, I looked back and forth between the screen and his face.{p}

On the screen were Tokita and the mummy.
"...That's amazing.
That's a really well-made mummy."
I honestly thought so.
It didn't look fake at all. It was as realistic as the real thing.{p}

"It's going to kill me!
If I don't stop it fast, the mummy's going to kill me!
Everyone dies.
Everyone who gets attacked in this film really dies!"
Tokita screamed in a trembling voice.
Honestly, I didn't understand.
And then, at that very moment,
he told me the secret of this film.
If someone told you something like that, could you believe it?
I'm sorry, but I couldn't.
People dying exactly the way it happened in a film? Surely not.
On the screen, Tokita was quaking with terror.
Just like the real one standing right in front of me...
"Eeeeek!"{p}

At last, he yanked out the plug.
But what do you think happened?{p}

The editing equipment was still running.
Even though he had pulled the plug.
"Aaaah!"
He clutched his head and crouched down right where he stood.
The Tokita on the screen was doing exactly the same thing.
After all, Tokita was the only one who knew the film's scenes.
I thought he was trying to scare me, so I did my best to stay calm.{p}

But it was right then.
Suddenly, a hand covered in bandages thrust out of the darkness and seized Tokita by the neck.
I couldn't do a thing.
It was all too much. I could only stand there, frozen.
Then, after the bandaged hand, a mummy with bandages wound around its face emerged from the darkness.
The eyeballs peering out between the roughly wound bandages were dull and clouded, like a dead fish's.{p}

"AAAAAAAAAGH!"
Tokita's death scream echoed through the audiovisual room.{p}

The mummy's hand gripped Tokita's head and crushed it.
The mummy crushed Tokita's head as easily as a mandarin orange.
What was left of Tokita, changed beyond recognition, looked like a split watermelon.
Even with his head crushed, Tokita's body was still twitching and trembling.{p}

I couldn't do anything. I just stood there.
When I suddenly came to my senses, the mummy was gone.
It had vanished, as if it had melted into the darkness.
All that was left behind was Tokita's corpse.{p}
And the editing screen showed Tokita lying dead in exactly the same pose, stopped on that very scene.
I ran.{p}
...Say, {a}.{p}Would you want to see that film?
I'd like to see it
I don't want to see it

I see.
I thought so.
You like horror films, after all.
You'd want to see just how incredible the footage on it was, I'm sure.
But you know, Tokita's death at school caused quite a stir, and yet the dozens of reels of film in the audiovisual room vanished without a trace, as if they had never been there at all.{p}

And with Tokita's death, the Film Research Society was disbanded too.
None of the Film Research Society's members knew anything about that film.
What was that film, I wonder?
If that film has been completed somewhere, I'd very much like to see it...{p}
By the way, I ended up taking one reel of that film with me.
Would you like to see just this one reel, at least?
I'd love to see it
I don't need to see it

I see.
But this is the one thing I can't show you.
The truth is, that scene was so incredible it was burned into my eyes, so I went to the trouble of buying an 8mm projector and watched it at home.
It was all there, clear as day.
The sight of Tokita being killed, just as I saw it with my own eyes.{p}

After that, I started watching the film at regular intervals.
As if I were observing it.
As the months went by, Tokita turned completely into a skeleton.
And before I knew it, there was no one on the screen anymore.
The bones were cleanly gone too, whether they'd crumbled away or someone had cleared them up.
Not a single bone was left.
Just the empty audiovisual room, shown flatly, on and on.
But when I looked closely, it wasn't so.
I was wrong to think no one was there.
Right beside the spot where Tokita's body had been, someone was standing blankly.{p}

...It was me.
As if it were reenacting what happened that day.
And behind me, an eerie bandaged hand was just about to reach out.
I hurriedly stopped the projector.
I wondered what I would do if it didn't stop, but luckily, it did.
That's why I'm still alive here today.
When I think of what would have happened if the machine hadn't stopped, like that time in the audiovisual room... it still makes my blood run cold.
That's why I will never watch that film again.
If I did, it would surely be my turn to die.
I can't bring myself to throw it away either, so I keep it carefully at the back of a drawer.{p}

All the while wondering what I'd do if someone ever watched it.
The terror of always living side by side with death... none of you could understand that, I suppose.
...That's how it always is for me.
Because of that living film.
Whether it's the mummy's curse or the film's curse, I can't tell.{p}

But what became of the film that disappeared back then?
Is it still passing from hand to hand, even now?
Maybe the reason people die is really no more than that.
Somewhere, someone quietly watches the footage of the moment you die.
It's a cursed film, after all.{p}

Perhaps it has changed its form.
Not 8mm film anymore, but a videotape...
And perhaps it has found its way into your home.
If you ever find an old videotape with no title label on it, be careful.
There's no guarantee that it's a tape of yours...
And with that, I'll end my story.{p}

I see.
To think there'd be another French-film lover here...
That's right.
French films choose their audience.
Even in my circle, film buff that I am, only two or three people can understand that poetic world.
Which makes you, {a}, one of those precious few.{p}
By the way, {a}, what other kinds of films do you like?{p}

...You dislike them?
I see. That's a shame.
French films do choose their audience, after all.
Whenever I ask people if they like French films, they all tell me the images are beautiful.
But most of them say they can't understand what the film is about, or what's so interesting about it...
Sadly...
By the way, {a}, could it be that you dislike movies in general?{p}

Well, well...
This is a golden opportunity to make another French-film lover.
There are all sorts of French films, you know.
Some don't go over well with ordinary audiences, but others have popular appeal.
Next time, I'll pick out some French films I recommend for you.
You have my guarantee.
You're sure to love them.{p}
By the way, {a}, what kinds of films do you like?{p}

You dislike them?
I think films are wonderful things, myself.{p}

Something ordinary, then...
Today, let me tell you about a student at this school named Tokita.{p}

He was the kind of student who would stay up all night watching films and then doze off at school.
It wasn't that the teachers never scolded him, but Tokita's grades were decent, so they mostly let it slide.
No matter how much you love films, there's only so much you can buy or rent on a high schooler's allowance.
So he recorded TV broadcasts himself, and asked friends who had satellite or cable TV at home to tape things for him.
Well, the friends who had gladly agreed at first gradually started finding it a hassle.
Still, maybe it was down to Tokita's good nature.
His friends only made half-joking snide remarks, and kept recording for him.
Then, one day...{p}

"Huh? There's no title..."
A few times before, he had borrowed tapes where someone had forgotten to write the title.
Each time, not knowing what was on them had driven him crazy.{p}This time too, he couldn't stop wondering about it.
Hurry home and check it
Check it in the audiovisual room

Curious about what was on it, he hurried home.
And once he got home, he checked the tape.{p}

The tape showed nothing but ordinary scenes of the school.
Tokita assumed it was a home video someone had shot.
"I'll ask around whose it is and give it back."
A film or a TV recording is one thing, but with home video footage, you feel guilty, as if you were peeking into someone's diary.
Thinking that, he put it in his bag.{p}

The next day at school, he asked the people who had recorded for him about the tape.
But none of them recognized it.
Tokita was at a loss, and searched hard for the owner.
Well, most people would just think it was fine to wait for someone to come forward.
I suppose that's why nobody ever disliked Tokita.
But in the end, the owner was never found.{p}

Then he went home.
Even at home, he couldn't stop thinking about the tape.
"Maybe if I watch what's on it, I'll find out whose it is."
Once he thought that, he was seized by the temptation to see what was on it.
He was so into films, after all, so maybe it was only natural that a devil would whisper to him to watch it.
Maybe there was a film recorded after the home video scenes he'd seen yesterday.
The more he imagined things like that, the more his desire to watch it swelled up inside him.
And at last, he put the video into the deck and decided to watch it.{p}

The footage showed the school grounds, the same as yesterday.
"Huh, I'm in this."
On the screen was Tokita himself, looking for the videotape's owner earlier that day.
"But this tape got mixed in with mine yesterday..."{p}

The video went on, and night fell.
"That's weird. It should still be light outside."
When he looked at his window, the evening sun was streaming in.
Tokita realized he had been assuming the video was shot today, and found it funny.
"How dumb can I be? There's no way this was shot today."
And the footage rolled on.{p}

Some kind of white figure appeared.
"Who's that?"
Tokita followed the footage.
The figure gradually grew clearer.{p}

"The Mummy Man... So this was a film after all?"
By now, he was in the mood for watching a film.
He was watching the cruel scenes unfolding on the video with an appreciative eye.
He had already broken free of the delusion that it was real footage of today.
Then the video ended.{p}

For a while, Tokita just sat there in a daze.
Because amid the clumsy direction, there had been scenes with a force unlike anything he had ever seen.
The Mummy Man had chased a high school girl and mercilessly torn her apart until she died.
"It must be an indie film.
If the school is the setting, someone connected with the school must have made it."
Once he thought that, he couldn't rest until he had found the tape's owner.
He wanted to see what came next... no, he wanted to see the finished film. With that thought, he went to bed.
And it was already starting to get light by the time he finally drifted off to sleep.{p}

Then, keeping his eyes on the ground, he hurried toward his classroom.
It was just as he was about to enter the school building.{p}

There on the ground, off in a corner, lay a scrap of bandage.
At that moment, Tokita understood.
The footage on that video had really happened.
And from then on, he couldn't get the scenes from that video out of his head.
Apparently the police investigated the murder as the work of a deranged person.
But Tokita alone was certain the truth of the case lay elsewhere.{p}

He went home and sat thinking in front of the video.
That tape had gotten mixed in with his the day before yesterday.
But the incident must have happened last night.
Then what was it that had been recorded on that tape?
Still, no matter how he thought about it, it had to be a scene of last night's murder.
I have to check, he thought.
And he played the video once more.{p}
A figure came into view.{p}

And then, the Mummy Man.
"Huh...?"{p}

This time, the one running for their life wasn't a high school girl.
It was a man... a police officer.
It was a scene of a police officer running for his life.
"This is strange. It's not what I saw yesterday."
And then the officer was killed, just like the high school girl the day before.
"A different tape...?"
That couldn't be.
"Maybe there are several scenes recorded on it..."
He checked the tape and rewound it, but it began with the same police officer scene.
And after that, there was nothing on it at all.{p}

He checked every video in his room, but the tape of the high school girl being killed was nowhere to be found.
Tokita went to the school at the same hour the officer had been killed on the tape.{p}

In the schoolyard, ropes had been strung up around the spot where the high school girl was killed.
There was no body at the spot where the officer had been killed in the video.
"Looks like it hasn't happened yet."
He was certain that a police officer was going to be killed.
And so Tokita waited.
He waited a long time.
But everything around him was hushed and still.
Now and then, a patrol car drove past.
"If I keep hanging around like this, they'll get suspicious of me."
It was just as he was about to head home.{p}

"Gyaaaah!"
It was a man's scream.
Tokita stared at the sight as if he were watching a scene from a movie.
I suppose he could no longer tell reality from the movies.{p}

From that day on, every night, he chased down the scenes recorded on the videotape.
Tokita no longer needed to ask his friends to record movies for him.{p}

"Hey, Tokita, you've stopped asking us to tape stuff for you lately."
"I found something much more interesting."
That's the kind of thing he said.
Then, one day, it happened.{p}

After school, he went home and watched the video, as always.
"I wonder what kind of scene it'll be today."{p}

The footage showed the school at night.
But suddenly, the picture went fuzzy and stopped.{p}

"Huh, that's weird... Well, as long as I know where it is."
With that in mind, he headed for the school that night.{p}

"It should be around here..."
Some time passed, but nothing happened.
"That's strange. Maybe nothing's happening today..."
And then, just as he turned around to go home...{p}

And then he died.
Hm? How do I know this story?
The truth is, that day I'd gone to his house to get back a tape I'd lent him earlier.
He wasn't home, but his mother showed me to his room and let me check his tapes.
And I saw it. Footage of him being killed.
At the time, just like him, I thought it was some amateur film or something and didn't think much of it.
But when night came, I couldn't get it out of my mind, so I went to the school to see.
And sure enough, it had already happened.
I don't know what became of that video afterward.
I wonder whose murder will show up on it next.
That's the end of my story.
Next person, please.{p}

I see.
So you like action?
You can really tell that action movies these days keep getting more and more extreme and intense.
And a lot of them are very well made, too.
